scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants the value of healthy doubt, then argues mistrusting every fact is unworkable; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: It is true that people once believed the earth was flat and that the sun moved around it.
One claim holds that any information called a fact should be mistrusted, on the reason that much supposedly factual information later turns out to be wrong.
I agree that we should question facts carefully, but I disagree that we should mistrust all of them.

sections.role: Body 1 — The value of healthy doubt

sentences.text: First, there is real value in the caution the claim recommends.
History shows that many confident beliefs were later proven completely false.
For example, doctors once treated patients in ways we now know were useless or even harmful.
This shows that treating every fact as certain can lead us into serious error.
A healthy doubt encourages people to test claims rather than accept them blindly.
Questioning supposed facts is exactly how science corrects its own mistakes.
To this extent, the reason behind the claim contains genuine wisdom.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why total mistrust is unworkable

sentences.text: Second, however, mistrusting every fact would make life and thought impossible.
We rely on countless dependable facts every day, from medicine to engineering, that have proven true again and again.
Consider that doubting whether bridges hold weight or whether medicines work would paralyse us completely.
Such total mistrust shows that the claim, taken seriously, would leave us unable to act at all.
The fact that some beliefs prove false does not mean that all facts are unreliable.
Most well-tested facts are trustworthy precisely because they have survived repeated questioning.
Wisdom lies, then, in questioning facts carefully rather than mistrusting them all.
In conclusion, we are right to question facts, since some of them do turn out to be wrong.
But mistrusting every fact would make knowledge and daily life impossible.
The wisest approach is to test facts carefully while still trusting those that have been well proven.
